learning_outcomes: Understand that matter is particulate and possesses mass and volume.
Explain characteristics of particles: continuous motion, attraction, inter-particle spaces.
Differentiate between the three common states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas.
Explain interconversion of states using temperature and pressure changes, latent heat.
Explain evaporation and its cooling effect.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: A change of state directly from solid to gas without changing into liquid state upon heating.
The amount of heat energy required to change 1 kg of a liquid into gas at atmospheric pressure at its boiling point.
The phenomenon of change of a liquid into vapours at any temperature below its boiling point.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Kinetic Molecular Theory of Matter
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: All matter consists of tiny particles in constant random motion possessing kinetic energy directly proportional to temperature.

key_diagrams: Interconversion of the three states of matter
Sublimation of Ammonium Chloride in China Dish

activities.title: Sublimation of Ammonium Chloride
activities.aim: To observe sublimation in ammonium chloride upon heating.
procedure: Take crushed ammonium chloride in a clean china dish.
Put an inverted glass funnel over the china dish.
Put a cotton plug on the stem of the funnel.
Heat slowly with a burner and observe.
precautions: Plug the funnel stem tightly with cotton to prevent escape of vapors.
Heat gently to prevent thermal cracking of the porcelain dish.
activities.observations: Solid ammonium chloride changes directly into white vapors which rise and condense on the cooler inner walls of the funnel as pure solid deposits.

summary_points: Matter exists in solid, liquid, and gaseous states.
Evaporation causes cooling due to absorption of latent heat from surroundings.

learning_outcomes: Distinguish between pure substances and mixtures (homogeneous and heterogeneous).
Understand properties of solutions, suspensions, and colloidal solutions.
Explain Tyndall effect and Brownian motion.
Calculate mass percentage and volume percentage of solutions.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles in a medium.
A heterogeneous mixture in which solute particles are intermediate in size (1 to 1000 nm) and remain uniformly dispersed.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Constant Proportions in Compounds
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: In a pure chemical compound, elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Mass \% of Solute} = \frac{\text{Mass of Solute}}{\text{Mass of Solution}} \times 100
\text{Volume \% of Solute} = \frac{\text{Volume of Solute}}{\text{Volume of Solution}} \times 100
\text{Mass of Solution} = \text{Mass of Solute} + \text{Mass of Solvent}

activities.title: Demonstration of Tyndall Effect in Colloidal Solutions
activities.aim: To observe the scattering of light (Tyndall effect) in a colloidal solution compared to a true solution.
procedure: In beaker A, prepare copper sulphate true solution in water.
In beaker B, prepare colloidal milk-water mixture.
Direct a focused light beam through both beakers from the side in a dark room.
Observe the path of light through both beakers.
precautions: Perform the experiment in a dimly lit or dark room for distinct visibility.
Do not look directly into the laser beam.
activities.observations: The path of light is not visible in the true solution (beaker A), but is clearly illuminated and visible in the colloidal milk solution (beaker B).
activities.conclusion: Colloidal particles are large enough to scatter visible light, displaying the Tyndall effect.

summary_points: Suspensions and colloids are heterogeneous mixtures.

learning_outcomes: State the Law of Conservation of Mass and Law of Constant Proportions.
Explain Dalton's Atomic Theory and its postulates.
Write chemical formulas using criss-cross valency method.
Calculate molecular mass and formula unit mass.
Understand the mole concept and Avogadro constant.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: One atomic mass unit is equal to exactly 1/12th of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
One mole of any species contains exactly 6.022 x 10^23 elementary particles.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Conservation of Mass
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Definite Proportions
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: In a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.

key_diagrams: Apparatus verifying law of conservation of mass in conical flask

activities.title: Verification of the Law of Conservation of Mass
activities.aim: To verify that total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a precipitation reaction.
procedure: Take 10 mL of sodium sulphate solution in the conical flask.
Take 5 mL of barium chloride solution in the ignition tube.
Suspend the ignition tube inside the flask with a thread without letting the two solutions mix, and cork the flask tightly.
Weigh the flask with its contents on the balance (initial mass m1).
Tilt and swirl the flask to mix the solutions thoroughly, forming white BaSO4 precipitate.
Weigh the flask again (final mass m2).
precautions: Cork the flask tightly so no vapor escapes.
Handle the balance carefully for precision.
activities.observations: A white precipitate of barium sulphate forms: m1 = m2 (no change in reading).
activities.conclusion: Mass is conserved in a chemical reaction: BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl.

summary_points: Atoms combine in whole numbers to form molecules and compounds.

learning_outcomes: Describe the discovery of subatomic particles: electron, proton, neutron.
Explain Thomson's plum pudding model, Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment, and Bohr's model.
Explain distribution of electrons in different orbits (Bohr-Bury scheme: 2n^2 rule).
Define atomic number (Z), mass number (A), valency, isotopes, and isobars.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The total number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom.
The sum of the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Bohr-Bury Scheme of Electronic Distribution
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: The maximum number of electrons in a shell of principal quantum number n is given by 2n^2, with outermost valence shell accommodating maximum 8 electrons.

key_formulas_and_equations: A = Z + N \implies N = A - Z
key_diagrams: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment setup and trajectories
Bohr's model of atom showing K, L, M, N energy levels

activities.title: Simulation of Alpha Particle Scattering
activities.aim: To understand Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom through alpha particle scattering observations.
procedure: Bombard a thin gold foil (about 1000 atoms thick) with fast-moving alpha particles.
Observe the scintillations on the circular fluorescent screen using detector.
Record angles of deflection and frequency of scattered particles.
precautions: Shield alpha source with lead container to avoid radiation hazard.
Conduct experiment in high vacuum chamber.
activities.observations: Most alpha particles pass straight through; a few are deflected by small angles; about 1 in 12,000 rebounds back at nearly 180 degrees.
activities.conclusion: Most of the space inside atom is empty; positive charge and nearly all mass is concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.

summary_points: An atom contains protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in discrete energy shells.

learning_outcomes: Distinguish between distance and displacement, speed and velocity.
Define uniform motion, non-uniform motion, and acceleration.
Derive equations of motion using graphical method.
Understand uniform circular motion and calculate speed.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The shortest straight-line distance measured from initial to final position of an object.
The rate of change of velocity with respect to time: a = (v - u) / t.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Kinematic Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: For motion along a straight line with constant acceleration a, relationships between initial velocity u, final velocity v, displacement s, and time t are given by the three equations of motion.

key_diagrams: Distance-time graph for uniform and non-uniform motion
Velocity-time graph for uniformly accelerated motion

activities.title: Measuring Average Speed and Velocity along an Inclined Plane
activities.title_te: వాలుతలంపై సరాసరి వేగం మరియు త్వరణాన్ని కొలవడం
activities.aim: To determine the acceleration of a marble rolling down an inclined plane using distance and time measurements.
procedure: Set up the grooved plank at a gentle slope using wooden blocks.
Mark points at 40 cm, 80 cm, 120 cm, 160 cm from the top release point.
Release the marble from rest at top and start stopwatch.
Measure time taken to reach each mark, repeating 3 times for average.
precautions: Release the ball gently without imparting any initial push.
Keep the angle of inclination small to reduce timing errors.
activities.observations: Distance traveled increases proportionally to square of time: s proportional to t^2, confirming constant acceleration.
activities.conclusion: The rolling ball undergoes uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion: a = 2s / t^2.

summary_points: Motion is relative to chosen reference point.
Acceleration is zero in uniform motion.

learning_outcomes: Explain balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects.
State Newton's First Law of Motion and define inertia and mass.
State Newton's Second Law of Motion and derive F = ma.
State Newton's Third Law of Motion and Law of Conservation of Momentum.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The natural tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.
The product of mass and velocity of an object: p = mv, with SI unit kg m/s.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Newton's First Law of Motion
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: An object remains in a state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change that state by an applied unbalanced force.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Newton's Second Law of Motion
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: The rate of change of momentum of an object is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of force: F = ma.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Newton's Third Law of Motion
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, and they act on two different bodies.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: In an isolated system, the total linear momentum before collision is equal to the total linear momentum after collision: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2.

key_formulas_and_equations: m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 \quad (\text{Conservation of Momentum})
key_diagrams: Coin dropping into glass when card is flicked (Inertia)
Two spring balances demonstrating equal and opposite action-reaction

activities.title: Demonstrating Newton's Third Law with Two Spring Balances
activities.title_te: రెండు స్ప్రింగ్ త్రాసులతో న్యూటన్ మూడవ నియమ నిరూపణ
activities.aim: To prove that action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction using two connected spring balances.
apparatus: Two identical spring balances A and B
procedure: Attach the ring of spring balance B to a rigid fixed hook on the wall.
Hook the free hook of spring balance A into the hook of balance B.
Pull the free ring end of balance A horizontally.
Observe and note down the force readings on both balances A and B simultaneously.
precautions: Ensure both spring balances are calibrated to read zero when relaxed.
Pull smoothly without jerking to maintain steady pointer reading.
activities.observations: Both spring balances show identical force readings in opposite directions.
activities.conclusion: Force exerted by A on B (action) equals force exerted by B on A (reaction) in opposite directions.

summary_points: Inertia depends on the mass of an object.
Linear momentum is conserved in all collisions.

learning_outcomes: State the Universal Law of Gravitation and its mathematical form.
Differentiate between acceleration due to gravity (g) and universal gravitational constant (G).
Distinguish between mass and weight.
Explain thrust and pressure, Archimedes' Principle, and relative density.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
When a body is immersed fully or partially in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force that is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Kepler's Three Laws of Planetary Motion
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus; Area vector sweeps equal areas in equal intervals of time; Square of orbital period is proportional to cube of semi-major axis: T^2 proportional to R^3.

key_formulas_and_equations: F = G\frac{M m}{d^2}, \quad G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2
\text{Relative Density} = \frac{\text{Density of Substance}}{\text{Density of Water at } 4^\circ\text{C}}
key_diagrams: Gravitational attraction between two masses M and m separated by distance d
Archimedes principle setup with eureka overflow can and measuring cylinder

activities.title: Verification of Archimedes' Principle
activities.aim: To verify that the buoyant force on a submerged body equals the weight of displaced liquid.
procedure: Fill Eureka can with water up to spout level until excess drains out.
Place dry measuring cylinder under spout.
Weigh the metal cylinder in air using spring balance (W1).
Lower cylinder gently into Eureka can and note spring balance reading (W2).
Measure volume and weight of displaced water in measuring cylinder (W_disp).
precautions: Ensure cylinder does not touch bottom or sides of overflow can.
Do not splash water while lowering the solid body.
activities.observations: Loss of weight (W1 - W2) equals weight of water collected in measuring cylinder (W_disp).
activities.conclusion: Buoyant force equals weight of fluid displaced, confirming Archimedes' Principle.

summary_points: Weight varies with local g, while mass remains constant throughout universe.
Bodies float when buoyant force equals their total weight.

learning_outcomes: Define scientific work, positive work, negative work, and zero work.
Explain kinetic energy, potential energy, and derive expressions.
State and prove the Law of Conservation of Energy.
Define power and commercial unit of electrical energy (kWh).

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: Work done on an object is defined as magnitude of force multiplied by displacement in the direction of force: W = F . s.
The energy possessed by an object on account of its motion: E_k = (1/2) m v^2.
The rate of doing work or rate of transfer of energy: P = W / t, unit Watt (W).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Conservation of Energy
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another. Total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

key_formulas_and_equations: E_p = m g h \quad (\text{Gravitational Potential Energy})
key_diagrams: Free fall of body showing transformation of potential energy into kinetic energy

activities.title: Demonstration of Transformation and Conservation of Mechanical Energy
activities.title_te: యాంత్రిక శక్తి పరివర్తన మరియు నిత్యత్వ ప్రదర్శన
activities.aim: To observe energy transformation in a simple pendulum and verify mechanical energy conservation.
procedure: Suspend bob from rigid stand using thread.
Pull bob aside to extreme position A at height h and release from rest.
Observe motion passing through mean position B to opposite extreme C.
Record velocity at lowest point B and maximum height attained at extremes.
precautions: Displace bob by small angle (less than 15 degrees) to maintain simple harmonic motion.
Ensure thread does not stretch or slip.
activities.observations: At extreme points, energy is purely potential (mgh); at lowest point, energy is purely kinetic (1/2 mv^2 = mgh).
activities.conclusion: Total mechanical energy E = E_k + E_p remains conserved at all points of oscillation.

summary_points: Work is done only when force causes displacement in its direction.
Total energy remains constant throughout all transformations.

learning_outcomes: Explain production and propagation of sound waves as mechanical longitudinal waves.
Describe characteristics: wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude, and pitch.
State laws of reflection of sound and conditions for echo and reverberation.
Explain applications of ultrasound (cleaning, crack detection, echocardiography, SONAR).

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions.
The number of complete sound wave oscillations per unit time, measured in Hertz (Hz).
Sound Navigation and Ranging: A technique using ultrasonic waves to measure distance, direction, and speed of underwater objects.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Laws of Reflection of Sound
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: The angle of incidence of sound equals the angle of reflection; incident sound wave, reflected wave, and normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

key_formulas_and_equations: 2d = v \times t \implies d = \frac{vt}{2} \quad (\text{Echo and SONAR Equation})
key_diagrams: Longitudinal sound wave showing compressions and rarefactions
Reflection of sound apparatus setup with two hollow tubes and clock

activities.title: Demonstrating the Laws of Reflection of Sound
activities.aim: To verify that the angle of incidence of sound equals the angle of reflection.
apparatus: Two identical hollow cardboard / plastic pipes (1 m long)
procedure: Place two hollow pipes at an angle facing the reflecting board.
Place a ticking watch near open end of pipe 1.
Listen through open end of pipe 2, adjusting its angle until ticking sound is heard loudest.
Measure angles made by both pipes with normal to reflecting board.
precautions: Ensure the room is completely quiet.
Place a vertical cardboard screen between the two pipes to prevent direct sound transmission.
activities.observations: The ticking sound is heard clearest and loudest when angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).
activities.conclusion: Sound obeys the laws of reflection similar to light.

summary_points: Sound requires a material medium to propagate.
Humans hear frequencies in audible range 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
